Cheap and easy adventure game, but not really a puzzle game. 

The game is fun for what it is, but it isn't what I expected at all. When I fired it up I thought it was going to be a much deeper experience. That isn't to say it wasn't enjoyable, it at the very minimum had some amazing atmosphere and music. It was fun for a bit to read through old IRC chat logs and relive its heyday. 

Most of the game is following instructions without question. This was never subverted, and everything was as simple as expected throughout the entire game. I was expecting a few missions where I edited records, or deleted files, to backfire, and I would have to restore those records or find another copy of the file, but nothing of the sort happened. I instead became super hackerman within 2 hours and with some software I downloaded I was able to break into just about every computer on the planet. The game in general isn't particularly hard, and if you know anything about unix commands, you can get through everything fairly quickly. If you lose or someone traces you the worst that happens is you reboot your virtual computer, and the most you lose out is some time but that is about it, so the stakes are about as low as possible. 

There were a few bugs, and few missions never triggered unless I followed a guide. That is the only reason I have 8 hours on the game, I beat it easily doing just about everything except the DLC in around 4 hours. It took me redoing a particular part twice to get the /el message board missions to trigger but if you ignore 100% completion read quickly, know your unix commands and stick to the main story, you can finish even faster.

I do have a few gripes though, for one the user tags at the moment say it is a simulation and programming game. However this can't be further from the truth. The tutorial at first used real unix commands to control your computer, and I was preparing for a much more "hardcore experience". However, the more that I played the more that I was disappointed with the puzzles. It took me until about an hour in before I realized it isn't a puzzle game at all. It really just an adventure game. Very few locks have time pressure and that is the hardest part of the game. Otherwise you just follow instructions and don't really think about what is going on.  The simulation aspects are fairly shallow, and at most the "hacking" is just run multiple programs, one after another. There is no programming at all, and I have no idea how why that is a tag. I think that some people misinterpret the terminal as programming. The terminal is something most people used to interact with computers up until the late 90s, and if you use Linux, you use it pretty much every day. Its just an alternate interface, it would be like calling using a mouse programming.

Pick it up on a deep sale if you want to kill some time, but there are other games that are much deeper and have more going on. The atmosphere is nice, and snooping through old IRC logs is worth the nostalgia alone, but if you have no interest in that, I would recommend for you to pass on this.

This game saved my life.

I am 27.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.

After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ing minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.

After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.

Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.

I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.

Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

This is essentially the perfect Hollywood hacking simulator.

Does this require you to be knowledgeable about anything even remotely related to computers? No.
Are you likely to have the craziest outro music when you inevitably die to an epileptic seizure the game gave you for doing nothing but clicking a single button? Yes.
Is the plot-twist of this game literally given away by, like, the first line of text you read after starting a new game? Maybe.

This game makes use of a small set of basic Linux commands and places you in the role of a hacker taking on interesting contracts. It's a very simple game and even players without any Linux or background in IT should be able to pick this up fairly easily. There's a good amount of puzzles or problem solving required (using logic and the tools that you're given) to progress through many of the missions that feel rewarding when you figure them out. I enjoyed reading the many logs with older memes from 10+ years ago thrown in. The IRC chat and snippets brought back lots of memories from my IRC days as a kid in the 90s. There are some very minor GUI improvements that could be made, but nothing that is annoying enough or game-breaking. The game still feels very immersive even as a more arcadey "hacking" game. Recommended!

For such a simple game with a couple of shell commands, it's really fun and gets increasingly complex to find and hack into places by the end. Kind of feels like breaking into places in Deus Ex 1, but if you were hacking and invading every complex via their network. 

Gripes: Console's a bit jank and sometimes the caret zooms around for no reason. DELETE doesn't work as expected (reverse backspace). Scrolling through previous commands zooms past too many too quickly sometimes.

Minor complaints though. It's easy to get hooked and enjoy messing around reading amusing IRC logs on random nodes you've hacked into. The game isn't too long but it doesn't overstay its welcome. Lots of fun for an 8 hour long game. Good stuff.

Summary: 
Hacknet is a terminal-based hacking simulator where you progress through the story of a dead hacker to right his wrongs. At it's core, Hacknet is essentially a forensic game loosely based in reality with impactful story moments. If you have any interest in cybersecurity/hacking, I HIGHLY recommend playing this game.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
Hacknet's gameplay can best be compared to using an extremely light version of Linux. You type commands (like in a real terminal) to execute programs to break through other computers defense systems and download, erase, or perform some minor forensics within. Forensics might entail noting a password in a txt file, scanning the network to find connected devices, and tracing other hackers' activity to a source. In the endgame, you even have the choice of killing or saving (Labyrinths DLC) people via hacking.

[h3]Achievements[/h3]
Only 11 achievements, none of which are difficult. Just make sure not to miss "Rude" by replying to the malicious hacker after he sends you an email ASAP.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story isn't terribly deep, but you do feel immersion in the world from the small connections in various conversations/txt files throughout. Some missions are quite impactful, multiplied by the OST's (or absence of) ability to evoke emotion. Labyrinths DLC is also a good story, condensed, and with a hint more memorability.

[h3]Hate[/h3]
Nothing to really hate, but if the devs were to see this, I'd recommend expanding and densifying things more. 
- The story could be more fleshed out via additional background on who was [spoiler]Bitwise[/spoiler], what he did, his background, etc. 
- The gameplay could be improved by further consultation with real cybersecurity experts in making the game even more realistic with more tools and mechanics. [b]One I'd personally love to see is creating your own malware so that you don't just play as a script kiddie with god-tier tools from the start.[/b]

Hacknet does a good job of abstracting the minutiae of real-world hacking that would normally go well over my head, and distilling it into an experience that was both very comprehensible and did a good job of making me feel the way I always hoped I would if I actually knew anything about hacking. There's not really any way to brute force progress in this game - you're given a set of tools, shown how to use them, and are trusted to apply them where relevant. These tools are drip-fed to the player so as not to overwhelm them with information which, now that think about it, kind of makes this game structured like a text-based metroidvania.

Though the hacking minigame remains engaging enough that it doesn't quite overstay its welcome throughout the length of the game, the real substance and joy of Hacknet is in following along with the narrative mystery, chasing down leads, finding the cracks in a target's security, and widening them. In this way, even though the gameplay and presentation are significantly different, I think that Hacknet deserves to be mentioned in the same breath as other great mystery games like Return of the Obra Dinn.

That's definitely not the original pitch of the game, but I do think it's a fair description of Hacknet: a (mostly) text-based metroidvania mystery game. If that sounds like it might be right up your alley, I highly recommend giving it a try.

Near the beginning of the game, I got hacked by another hacker. I was unable to react in time to shut down my own computer or whatever, so the guy got into my computer. However, instead of being greeted with a game over screen, the computer rebooted to the terminal. After doing a little digging, manually navigating my files with command prompts, I discovered the guy deleted the part of the Hacknet OS that used the UI. So, I somehow managed to connect to another computer on my network, and downloaded the file from there. When I rebooted, the UI was completely different from the one I was using before, new colours and such. I went onto my computer, looked at the logs, and discovered that the guy hadn't cleared them, so I connected to his IP and was rewarded with a cool software a bit earlier in the game than you're supposed to get it.

This experience blew my mind. It was incredibly reactive and clever. I only wish the whole game was like that, but the vast majority of it is just "go into this computer, type a thing, wait a bit for the game to do the hacking for you, and then look at some files". The gameplay loop is repetitive, but doesn't overstay it's welcome. Sometimes you get new mechanics, but it basically just boils down to typing a different thing in the command prompt window (unless you play the DLC, which is a bit more involved). The writing is decent, sometimes you come across a funny file or an emotional side quest, but what really makes this game is it's music and visuals. The high energy electronic music and the cool animations that appear every time you run a program give the game an incredibly fun atmosphere that really does make you feel like a master hacker.

Overall, if you like games for the gameplay, maybe skip this one, but if you appreciate good music and can stomach quite a bit of reading, then you'll probably enjoy this game. I sure did.
